questions.stem: A nurse is teaching the parents of a 2-year-old about preventing choking. Which foods should the nurse identify as choking hazards that need to be modified or avoided for this child? Select all that apply.
opts: Whole nuts
Mashed sweet potato
Plain whole-milk yogurt
Whole grapes
Hot dog slices cut into rounds
Popcorn
questions.rat: Round, firm, or hard foods that match the size of a toddler's airway are the classic high-risk choking foods: whole grapes, hot dogs cut into rounds (which form a plug), popcorn, and whole nuts. Grapes and hot dogs should be cut lengthwise into small pieces. Mashed sweet potato and yogurt are soft, smooth textures that pose no choking risk.
questions.strat: Choking risk = round, firm, slippery, airway-sized — grapes, hot dogs, nuts, popcorn; soft/mashed is safe.
questions.why: Whole nuts, whole grapes, hot dog rounds, and popcorn are round, firm, airway-shaped foods that classically plug a toddler's airway. Grapes and hot dogs need to be cut lengthwise into small pieces rather than served whole or in rounds. Popcorn and whole nuts are avoided entirely at this age rather than modified.
whyNot: Mashed sweet potato is a soft, smooth texture with no round or firm pieces, so it poses no choking risk.
Plain whole-milk yogurt is a smooth, easily swallowed food that does not need to be modified for choking safety.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews a typical school day for an 8-year-old: skips breakfast, drinks two 12-oz sodas, eats a school lunch, and has chips after school. The parent says the child is often tired and inattentive at school. Which dietary change should the nurse recommend addressing first?
opts: Add a fiber supplement to the diet to improve bowel regularity
Begin a children's chewable calcium tablet every morning
Switch the salted after-school chips to baked vegetable chips
Start a daily breakfast and swap the sodas for water or milk
questions.rat: Eating breakfast daily is linked to better academic performance and behavior, and sugar-sweetened beverages are a leading source of empty calories in children, so adding breakfast and cutting the sodas targets the two highest-yield problems explaining the fatigue and inattention. A fiber supplement, a chip swap, and a calcium tablet address lower-priority or unrelated concerns and do not fix the missed morning meal or the sugar load.
questions.strat: School-age red flags: skipped breakfast + sugary drinks — fix those before fine-tuning snacks.
questions.why: Eating breakfast daily is linked to better academic performance and behavior, and sugar-sweetened sodas are a leading source of empty calories in children. Adding a daily breakfast and cutting the two sodas targets the two highest-yield problems behind this child's fatigue and inattention at school.
whyNot: A fiber supplement might help bowel regularity, but it does not address the missed breakfast or the sugar load driving the fatigue.
A chewable calcium tablet does not fix the missed morning meal or the two daily sodas contributing to inattention.
Swapping to baked chips improves a lower-priority snack choice but leaves the skipped breakfast and sugary drinks unaddressed.

questions.stem: The nurse counsels a 15-year-old female who is in her growth spurt. To support building bone mass, the priority nutrients are calcium and [1]. Because she is menstruating, the nurse also emphasizes adequate [2] intake to support growth, blood volume, and immunity.

blanks.label: [1] Bone-building partner nutrient
opts: vitamin C
vitamin K
vitamin D

blanks.label: [2] Nutrient especially needed by menstruating females
opts: folate
zinc
iron

questions.rat: Calcium and vitamin D together are critical during adolescence because nearly all bone mass is laid down by age 18; vitamin D drives calcium absorption. Menstruating adolescent females are at elevated risk for iron deficiency, and iron supports growth, blood volume, immunity, and cognitive development. Vitamin C, K, zinc, and folate matter generally but are not the targeted answers here.
questions.strat: Teen bone mass = calcium + vitamin D; menstruating teen = watch iron.
questions.why: Calcium and vitamin D together are critical during adolescence because nearly all bone mass is laid down by age 18. Vitamin D drives how well that calcium gets absorbed into bone. Because this client is menstruating, iron becomes the second priority, since it supports growth, blood volume, immunity, and cognitive development.

questions.stem: A school nurse evaluates a 16-year-old gymnast whose mother reports concerns about her eating. For each finding, indicate whether it is an Expected adolescent finding or a Concerning finding that warrants further assessment for a possible eating disorder.

rows.t: Going to the bathroom immediately after most meals
Occasionally choosing a vegetarian meal at lunch
Has stopped menstruating despite continued intense training
Increased appetite during a growth spurt
Wearing baggy layers and refusing to eat in front of others

questions.rat: Increased appetite during a growth spurt and an occasional vegetarian meal are normal. Self-induced behaviors and warning signs of an eating disorder include disappearing to the bathroom after eating (possible purging), concealing the body and avoiding eating around others, and amenorrhea from low energy availability, which is a recognized complication of weight-control practices in lean-sport athletes. These warrant nonjudgmental further assessment.
questions.strat: Eating-disorder red flags: bathroom after meals, hiding the body, amenorrhea — appetite and a veggie lunch are normal.
questions.why: Increased appetite during a growth spurt and an occasional vegetarian meal are both normal adolescent variations and not warning signs. Disappearing to the bathroom after eating, concealing the body, and avoiding eating around others are recognized warning signs. Amenorrhea from low energy availability is a known complication in lean-sport athletes and also warrants assessment.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old has a BMI in the 95th percentile for age and sex. The parents ask the nurse how to help. Which approach best reflects evidence-based, family-centered teaching for childhood overweight?
opts: Have the whole family adopt healthier meals and active routines together
Limit the child to one meal a day until the weight comes down
Tell the child to weigh daily and record everything that is eaten
Put the child on a calorie-restricted diet separate from the rest of the family
questions.rat: Family-based interventions are the evidence-based approach: the family environment shapes a child's eating attitudes and behaviors, so changing meals and activity for the whole household supports the child without shaming or singling them out. Isolating the child on a restrictive diet, mandating daily self-weighing and food logging, and skipping meals are stigmatizing or unsafe and can promote disordered eating in a growing child.
questions.strat: Childhood obesity teaching is family-wide and non-shaming — never isolate or starve the child.
questions.why: Family-based intervention is the evidence-based approach to childhood overweight because the family environment shapes a child's eating attitudes and behaviors. Changing meals and activity for the whole household supports this 10-year-old without singling him out or shaming him for his weight.
whyNot: Limiting a growing child to one meal a day is unsafe restriction that can trigger disordered eating patterns.
Mandating daily self-weighing and food logging places adult-level scrutiny on a child and can promote body shame.
Isolating the child on a separate restrictive diet singles him out from the family and can feel stigmatizing.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old client with a sedentary lifestyle and a BMI in the overweight range says, "I want to eat better to lower my risk of heart disease and diabetes." Using the Dietary Guidelines for Americans, which change should the nurse recommend the client focus on first?
opts: Add a daily multivitamin and otherwise keep the current eating pattern unchanged
Switch to a very high-protein plan and skip one meal each day to force a deficit
Eat more produce while cutting back on refined grains, added sugar, and sodium
Cut nearly all dietary fat and replace those calories with extra grains and bread
questions.rat: The Guidelines emphasize small shifts toward nutrient-dense foods, more produce, and less refined grains, added sugar, and sodium to lower diet-related chronic disease risk. Eliminating all fat and piling on grains misapplies the guidance; skipping meals on a high-protein plan is a fad approach, not a balanced pattern; a supplement does not fix an unbalanced base diet.
questions.strat: Chronic-disease prevention = shift the whole eating pattern toward nutrient density, not one magic fix.
questions.why: The Dietary Guidelines for Americans emphasize small, sustainable shifts toward nutrient-dense foods, including more produce and less refined grain, added sugar, and sodium. For this sedentary, overweight client, that whole-pattern shift is the recommended first step to lower chronic-disease risk.
whyNot: A multivitamin does not fix an unbalanced base diet, and it leaves the actual eating pattern unchanged.
Skipping meals on a very high-protein plan is a fad approach, not the balanced pattern the guidelines recommend.
Eliminating nearly all fat and adding extra grains misapplies the guidance and does not target the sugar or sodium problem.

questions.topic: Older Adult Energy vs. Nutrient Needs
questions.stem: The nurse teaches a 77-year-old client about age-related nutrition changes. As a person ages, total daily calorie needs generally [1], while the need for most vitamins and minerals [2]. Because of this combination, the nurse should counsel the client to prioritize [3].

blanks.label: [1] Calorie needs
opts: decrease
stay the highest of any life stage
increase

blanks.label: [2] Nutrient needs
opts: fall sharply as well
stay the same or increase
no longer apply

blanks.label: [3] Counseling focus
opts: larger total portion sizes
nutrient-dense foods over empty calories
extra refined grains for energy

questions.rat: With aging, metabolism and energy needs decline while requirements for most nutrients stay the same or rise, so each calorie must carry more nutrition; nutrient-dense foods meet needs without excess calories. Larger portions or refined grains add calories without proportional nutrients, widening the mismatch.
questions.strat: Aging = fewer calories, same/more nutrients, so every bite has to count (nutrient density).
questions.why: As people age, total daily calorie needs generally decline while the requirement for most vitamins and minerals stays the same or even increases. Because of this mismatch, this 77-year-old client should prioritize nutrient-dense foods so that every calorie consumed still delivers adequate vitamins and minerals.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old client living alone is admitted with new confusion, dry mucous membranes, and dark concentrated urine. The client says, "I just don't feel thirsty anymore, so I forget to drink." Which age-related change best explains this client's risk?
opts: A rising filtration rate that steadily flushes out body water and salt
A blunted thirst sensation that lets fluid deficits build unnoticed
An elevated metabolic rate that raises the client's baseline fluid needs
A heightened thirst drive that pushes the client toward overhydration
questions.rat: Older adults have a blunted thirst sensation, so they under-drink and slip into dehydration before noticing, which matches this client's findings. Glomerular filtration falls with age rather than rising, thirst is decreased rather than heightened, and metabolic rate declines rather than climbing.
questions.strat: Old + confused + dry membranes = think dehydration; the missing thirst cue is the trap.
questions.why: Older adults develop a blunted thirst sensation, so they under-drink and slip into dehydration before they consciously notice it. That mechanism matches this 80-year-old's new confusion, dry mucous membranes, and dark concentrated urine after living alone and forgetting to drink.
whyNot: Glomerular filtration rate actually falls with age rather than rising, so it does not explain this presentation.
Metabolic rate declines with age rather than climbing, so an elevated rate is not the mechanism at work here.
Thirst is decreased rather than heightened in older adults, so this option describes the opposite of what actually happens.

questions.topic: Malnutrition Risk Factors in Older Adults
questions.stem: A community-health nurse screens older adults living independently for malnutrition risk. Which findings should the nurse identify as increasing an older adult's risk for malnutrition? Select all that apply.
opts: Has several missing teeth and difficulty chewing many foods
Takes multiple medications that cause dry mouth and low appetite
Walks daily with neighbors and shares cooked meals on weekends
Lives alone and reports eating most meals in isolation
Keeps the home stocked with a variety of fresh and frozen foods
Relies on a fixed income and skips food to afford other bills
questions.rat: Social isolation, food insecurity on a fixed income, chewing problems, and polypharmacy with xerostomic or appetite-suppressing side effects all reduce intake and raise malnutrition risk in older adults. Regular social meals with neighbors and a well-stocked variety of food are protective, not risk factors.
questions.strat: Elder malnutrition is mostly social and functional: isolation, money, teeth, meds. The two protective options are the odd ones out.
questions.why: Social isolation, food insecurity on a fixed income, chewing problems from missing teeth, and polypharmacy causing dry mouth or low appetite all reduce food intake. Each factor interferes with either the ability or the desire to eat enough, raising this older adult's malnutrition risk.
whyNot: Walking daily with neighbors and sharing weekend meals is a social, protective habit, not a malnutrition risk factor.
A home stocked with a variety of fresh and frozen foods supports adequate nutrition rather than threatening it.

questions.stem: A 75-year-old client asks which nutrients older adults most often fall short on, given the age-related decline in nutrient absorption and synthesis. The nurse's teaching should highlight which pair as commonly inadequate in this age group?
opts: Vitamin C and vitamin K
Vitamin B12 and vitamin D
The minerals sodium and chloride
The B vitamins niacin and biotin
questions.rat: Aging reduces the ability to absorb and synthesize nutrients, leaving older adults at particular risk for inadequate vitamin B12 and vitamin D. Vitamins C and K, niacin/biotin, and sodium/chloride are not the classic at-risk nutrients of aging, and sodium is more often consumed in excess.
questions.strat: Older-adult deficiency pair to memorize: B12 and D.
questions.why: Aging reduces the body's ability to absorb and synthesize nutrients, which leaves older adults particularly prone to inadequate vitamin B12 and vitamin D. These two are the classic pairing nurses should highlight when teaching this 75-year-old about age-related deficiency risk.
whyNot: Vitamin C and vitamin K are not the nutrients classically tied to age-related absorption and synthesis decline.
Sodium and chloride are minerals that older adults more often over-consume, not fall short on with aging.
Niacin and biotin are not the classic at-risk nutrient pair associated with the aging process.

questions.stem: A nurse cares for an older client with Parkinson's disease who coughs and has a wet, gurgly voice after sips of thin tea. The client lives alone and prefers soft foods. Which action should the nurse prioritize?
opts: Have the client recline at a 30-degree angle while eating to ease swallowing
Encourage extra thin liquids between meals so the client stays hydrated
Request a professional swallowing evaluation before more oral intake
Add hard raw vegetables to meals to help strengthen the chewing muscles
questions.rat: Coughing and a wet, gurgly voice after thin liquids are warning signs of dysphagia and aspiration risk; a swallowing evaluation guides safe texture modification and must come before more oral intake (safety, assess-before-intervene). Pushing thin liquids, reclining while eating, and hard raw foods each increase aspiration or choking risk.
questions.strat: Wet voice + cough after liquids = dysphagia red flag; stop and get a swallow eval before feeding more.
questions.why: Coughing and a wet, gurgly voice after thin liquids are warning signs of dysphagia and aspiration risk in this client with Parkinson's disease. A formal swallowing evaluation must come before offering more oral intake so any texture modification is based on the client's actual ability.
whyNot: Reclining at only 30 degrees during eating actually increases aspiration risk rather than easing safe swallowing for this client.
Pushing more thin liquids is exactly what triggered the coughing and wet voice, so it raises aspiration risk further.
Hard raw vegetables are a choking hazard for a client already showing swallowing difficulty, not a safe strengthening tool.

questions.stem:
A home care nurse assesses a three-generation household at one visit. Which family member needs the nurse's follow-up FIRST for a current nutrition-related problem?

- A 33-year-old who is 9 weeks pregnant and continues eating sushi and sashimi made with raw fish
- An 8-year-old who avoids all dairy products but is offered other foods at meals
- An 11-year-old who eats fruit and carrots but refuses most other vegetables
- A 34-year-old in good health who eats a varied, balanced diet
opts: The 34-year-old healthy parent who eats a balanced, varied diet
The 8-year-old who avoids all dairy but is offered other foods
The 11-year-old who refuses most vegetables but does eat fruit
The 33-year-old who is 9 weeks pregnant and eating raw fish
questions.rat: Raw fish in pregnancy carries a real, immediate risk to mother and fetus (Listeria, mercury, parasites), so the pregnant client with an active harmful behavior is the current problem needing follow-up first. The dairy-avoiding child and the vegetable-refusing child are at risk for deficiency over time but are still being offered adequate alternatives, and the healthy parent has no nutritional concern.
questions.strat: Acute, active harm to two clients (mother + fetus) outranks a slow-developing single-nutrient risk.
questions.why: Raw fish in pregnancy carries an immediate risk to both the pregnant client and the fetus from Listeria, mercury, and parasites. That makes this an active, current harm rather than a slowly developing one, so she needs the nurse's follow-up first.
whyNot: The healthy 34-year-old parent eating a balanced, varied diet has no nutritional concern that needs follow-up at all.
The dairy-avoiding child is at risk for a slow-developing calcium shortfall, but is still being offered adequate alternative foods.
The vegetable-refusing child still eats fruit, so this is a slow, single-nutrient risk rather than an acute problem.

questions.stem: A client who is 9 weeks pregnant tells the nurse that sushi, poke, and sashimi are her favorite foods and part of her family's culture. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
opts: "Let's find cooked versions of those dishes so you can keep your traditions safely."
"Eating raw fish is a personal choice, so keep enjoying the dishes if they matter to you."
"Those raw dishes are fine in small amounts as long as you eat them only about once a week."
"You will need to give up those favorite dishes entirely until well after the baby is born."
questions.rat: Effective teaching pairs the safety rule (avoid raw fish in pregnancy) with the client's culture by adapting dishes to cooked versions, supporting both adherence and cultural identity. Telling her to give up the dishes entirely is unnecessary since cooked versions are safe; permitting small or weekly amounts of raw fish is still unsafe; and endorsing continued raw fish ignores the fetal risk.
questions.strat: Best teaching keeps the client's culture while changing only the unsafe part - adapt, don't forbid.
questions.why: Effective teaching pairs the safety rule against raw fish in pregnancy with this client's stated cultural identity by adapting her favorite dishes into cooked versions. That approach supports both adherence to the food-safety guidance and respect for the family traditions she named.
whyNot: Endorsing continued raw fish consumption ignores the real risk it poses to the developing fetus.
Permitting small or weekly amounts of raw fish is still unsafe, since the risk is not dose-dependent in that way.
Telling her to give up the dishes entirely is unnecessarily harsh since cooked versions are a safe substitute.

questions.stem: The nurse plans nutrition teaching tailored to each household member's life stage and situation. Indicate whether each strategy is Appropriate or Not appropriate as written.

rows.t: For the 82-year-old with moderate dementia, serve only 1 to 2 foods at a time and allow extra time to eat
For the 8-year-old who avoids dairy, offer calcium-fortified foods such as orange juice and bread
For the 11-year-old who dislikes vegetables, withhold preferred fruits until she eats her vegetables
For the 88-year-old with hypertension, teach the DASH eating plan and adapt it to his cultural dishes
For the 88-year-old with hypertension, advise him to salt foods to taste since intake naturally drops with age

questions.rat: Simplifying meals and allowing extra time fits dementia care; fortified foods meet the dairy-avoiding child's calcium needs; and culturally adapted DASH teaching supports the older adult with hypertension. Withholding preferred foods as leverage creates power struggles and is not recommended for children, and encouraging added salt directly contradicts the low-sodium goal for hypertension.
questions.strat: Tailor the stage: simplify for dementia, fortify for the picky eater, never bargain with food with kids.
questions.why: Simplifying meals and allowing extra time fits dementia care. Fortified foods meet a dairy-avoiding child's calcium needs. Culturally adapted DASH teaching supports an older adult managing hypertension. Withholding preferred foods as leverage creates power struggles and is not recommended with children, and encouraging added salt directly contradicts a low-sodium goal.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old client with hypertension wears full dentures and is starting the DASH eating plan. Which actions should the nurse include to support his nutrition and adherence? Select all that apply.
opts: Teach that red meats and sweets are allowed in small amounts
Arrange a dental evaluation to refit his dentures for chewing
Adapt the low-sodium plan to his cultural food preferences
Emphasize fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy
Have him eliminate all dairy products to lower sodium intake
Tell him to add table salt to improve the taste of bland foods
questions.rat: DASH emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while allowing red meat and sweets in small amounts, and adapting it to culture improves adherence. Refitting dentures supports chewing and intake in an older adult. Eliminating all dairy is wrong - low-fat dairy is a DASH component - and adding table salt undermines the low-sodium goal.
questions.strat: DASH limits sodium, not dairy; fix the dentures so the older adult can actually eat the plan.
questions.why: DASH emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while still allowing red meat and sweets in small amounts. Adapting the plan to this client's culture improves his adherence to it. Refitting his dentures also supports his ability to actually chew the foods DASH requires.
whyNot: Eliminating all dairy is incorrect since low-fat dairy is a core DASH component, not something the plan removes.
Adding table salt for flavor directly undermines the low-sodium goal that DASH is built around.

questions.stem: Six months after nutrition teaching, the nurse evaluates a pregnant client's progress. She gained 4 pounds in the first trimester, then about 1 pound per week, for a total of 33 pounds from her pre-pregnancy weight, and she avoids raw fish. Which conclusion is best supported?
opts: Weight gain is acceptable but raw-fish avoidance shows the teaching about safe foods failed
The total weight gain is excessive and the client should restrict calories for the rest of the pregnancy
Gestational weight gain and food safety are within expected limits; reinforce current habits
The first-trimester gain was inadequate and indicates poor fetal growth that needs urgent referral
questions.rat: A modest first-trimester gain followed by roughly 1 pound per week, totaling about 33 pounds, falls within the normal range for a single pregnancy, and avoiding raw fish shows the safety teaching worked - so the plan is effective and should be reinforced. The total is not excessive, the early gain is normal rather than a growth emergency, and avoiding raw fish is the desired outcome, not a failure.
questions.strat: On an outcome question, compare the data to the expected pattern before calling it a problem.
questions.why: A modest 4-pound first-trimester gain followed by about a pound per week, totaling 33 pounds, falls within the normal range for this pregnancy. Combined with her avoidance of raw fish, this shows the teaching worked and current habits should be reinforced.
whyNot: The weight gain here is normal, and avoiding raw fish is exactly the desired outcome, not a teaching failure.
A total gain of about 33 pounds falls within the normal range and is not excessive for this pregnancy.
A modest early gain followed by steady weekly weight gain is a normal pattern, not a growth emergency.

questions.stem:
A community nurse reviews recommended daily iron intake across several clients: a 2-year-old toddler (7 mg), a 16-year-old female (15 mg), a 30-year-old pregnant client (27 mg), and a 70-year-old man (8 mg).

Which client has the highest recommended iron intake, and what best explains it?
opts: The pregnant client, because iron must support expanded maternal blood volume and fetal needs
The 16-year-old female, because the pubertal growth spurt is the period of greatest iron demand
The 70-year-old man, because slowed peristalsis reduces iron absorption with age
The toddler, because rapid early growth makes iron the limiting nutrient for development
questions.rat: Pregnancy carries the highest recommended iron intake (27 mg) because iron supports the expanded maternal blood volume and the developing fetus. The adolescent female (15 mg) is high but second; the toddler (7 mg) is comparatively low; and reduced absorption in older adults raises intake needs in theory but the recommendation actually drops to 8 mg.
questions.strat: When a need peaks, ask what physiologic demand is being added — pregnancy adds a whole second circulation.
questions.why: Pregnancy carries the highest recommended iron intake, 27 mg daily, because iron must support both the expanded maternal blood volume and the developing fetus. The 16-year-old female's 15 mg is high but second, while the toddler's 7 mg and the 70-year-old man's 8 mg are comparatively low.
whyNot: The adolescent female's iron need is high at 15 mg, but it is still lower than the pregnant client's 27 mg.
Reduced absorption in older adults raises need in theory, but the actual recommendation drops to 8 mg after age 50.
The toddler's need is comparatively low at 7 mg, well below what pregnancy or adolescence requires.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches that nutritional priorities shift across the lifespan because the body's demands change. Recommended iron intake for females is [1] from the toddler years to mid-adolescence, and the recommendation for a non-pregnant woman then [2] after menopause. The factor that most directly drives the higher need during the reproductive years is [3].

blanks.label: [1] Toddler → adolescence
opts: roughly doubles
stays the same
is cut in half

blanks.label: [2] After menopause
opts: is unchanged
falls back toward childhood levels
rises sharply

blanks.label: [3] Main driver in reproductive years
opts: menstrual iron losses
lower physical activity
declining stomach acid

questions.rat: Female iron need rises from 7 mg (toddler) to 15 mg (14–18 yr), roughly doubling, then drops to 8 mg at age 51+ as menstrual losses end. The elevated requirement through the reproductive years is driven chiefly by recurring menstrual blood loss, not by acid changes or activity level.
questions.strat: Track a single nutrient up and down the age columns — the inflection points reveal the physiology.
questions.why: Recommended iron intake for females roughly doubles, rising from 7 mg in the toddler years to 15 mg by mid-adolescence. It then drops to 8 mg after age 51 as menstrual losses end. The elevated requirement across the reproductive years is driven chiefly by recurring menstrual blood loss, not by stomach-acid changes or activity level.

questions.stem:
A nurse plans foodborne-illness teaching for a community center serving people of all ages. Which individuals should be identified as being at HIGHER risk for serious foodborne illness and prioritized for teaching?

Select all that apply.
opts: A client receiving chemotherapy
An adult aged 65 and older
A healthy, active 25-year-old
A client who is pregnant
A child under 5 years of age
questions.rat: The four higher-risk groups span the lifespan and share weakened or altered defenses: young children (developing immunity, less stomach acid), older adults (declining immunity, slowed peristalsis, reduced liver/kidney clearance), the immunocompromised, and pregnant clients (altered immunity plus fetal risk). A healthy young adult is not in a designated high-risk group.
questions.strat: Foodborne risk clusters at the extremes of age and wherever defenses are altered — pregnancy and immune suppression.
questions.why: Young children, older adults, immunocompromised clients such as those on chemotherapy, and pregnant clients all share weakened or altered defenses against foodborne pathogens. Children have developing immunity and less stomach acid, older adults have declining immunity and slower peristalsis, and pregnancy alters immunity while adding fetal risk.
whyNot: A healthy, active 25-year-old has normal, intact immune defenses and is not in any designated high-risk group.

questions.stem:
A nurse is developing food-asphyxiation prevention materials and explains that choking risk is not evenly distributed across the lifespan.

Which statement best reflects how this risk is distributed?
opts: Risk climbs steadily with advancing age and peaks in middle adulthood
Only toddlers are at real risk, since adults chew and swallow maturely
School-age children carry the highest risk, which then declines with age
Both toddlers and older adults face elevated risk, from different causes
questions.rat: Choking can occur at any age, but risk concentrates at two ends of the lifespan: toddlers, whose chewing and swallowing skills are still developing, and older adults, in whom advanced age and coexisting conditions raise both the likelihood and the lethality of an event. It is not limited to toddlers, nor does it peak in school-age children or middle adulthood.
questions.strat: When risk is 'U-shaped' across age, name the distinct mechanism at each end rather than picking one group.
questions.why: Choking risk concentrates at two ends of the lifespan for different reasons. Toddlers are still developing chewing and swallowing skills. Older adults face elevated risk because advanced age and coexisting conditions raise both the likelihood and the lethality of an event. Naming both groups and their distinct mechanisms best fits this U-shaped pattern.
whyNot: Risk does not climb steadily with age or peak in middle adulthood, since it is elevated at both ends of life instead.
Choking is not limited to toddlers, since older adults also face elevated risk, just from different underlying causes.
School-age children are not the peak-risk group, and risk does not simply decline afterward through adulthood.

questions.stem:
A nurse refers clients to federal nutrition assistance programs. A low-income client who is pregnant asks which program is designed specifically for her life stage and that of her future infant.

Which program is the most appropriate referral?
opts: The Emergency Food Assistance Program (TEFAP), distributed through state food banks
Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), which targets pregnancy and early childhood
Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits for grocery purchases
The National School Lunch Program (NSLP), which serves enrolled school-age children
questions.rat: WIC is the program targeted to a specific lifespan window — low-income pregnant, breastfeeding, and postpartum women, plus infants and children up to age 5 at nutritional risk — providing supplemental foods, referrals, and nutrition education. NSLP serves school-age children, while SNAP and TEFAP address food insecurity broadly without targeting this stage.
questions.strat: Match the program to the life stage in its name — WIC literally names Women, Infants, and Children.
questions.why: WIC is the federal program targeted specifically to this client's life stage. It serves low-income pregnant, breastfeeding, and postpartum women, along with infants and children up to age 5 who are at nutritional risk. It provides supplemental foods, healthcare referrals, and nutrition education matched to pregnancy and early childhood.
whyNot: TEFAP distributes emergency food broadly through food banks but does not target this pregnancy-and-infancy life stage specifically.
SNAP addresses general food insecurity for grocery purchases but is not designed around any one life stage.
NSLP serves enrolled school-age children, which is a later life stage than this pregnant client's current need.

questions.stem:
During the anthropometric portion of a nutritional assessment, the nurse reviews an older adult's weight history. The client weighed 60 kg one month ago and weighs 54 kg today.

Enter the percent of weight change over the past month (round to the nearest whole number).
questions.rat: Percent weight change = weight lost ÷ original weight × 100 = 6 ÷ 60 × 100 = 10%. Percent of weight change over a given time period is the anthropometric data point the guide lists for the 'A' of the ABCDs, and an unintentional loss of this size flags the client for further nutritional evaluation.
questions.strat: Always divide by the ORIGINAL (earlier) weight, not the current weight, when computing percent change.
questions.why: Percent weight change equals weight lost divided by the original weight, times 100: 6 kg divided by 60 kg times 100 equals 10%. Percent weight change over time is the anthropometric data point in the ABCD framework. A loss this size flags this older adult for further nutritional evaluation.

questions.stem:
The nurse is monitoring the protein status of a client receiving a nutrition intervention. Serial biochemical (laboratory) values are recorded:

• Admission: albumin 2.6 g/dL, prealbumin 9 mg/dL
• Week 2: albumin 3.0 g/dL, prealbumin 14 mg/dL
• Week 4: albumin 3.4 g/dL, prealbumin 19 mg/dL

Which interpretation of this trend is most accurate?
opts: The protein markers are falling over time, so the client's protein status is steadily worsening
The values are all within normal limits, so no nutritional concern was present on admission
The values mainly reflect kidney function rather than protein status and therefore should not be trended
The protein markers are rising over time, so the nutrition intervention is improving protein status
questions.rat: Albumin and prealbumin are the protein markers the guide places in the biochemical ('B') category, used to determine nutritional deficiencies; tracking them over time is an anthropometric/biochemical evaluation outcome. Both values rise steadily across the three timepoints, indicating improving protein status and a working intervention. They are not falling, were clearly low on admission, and are protein — not renal — markers.
questions.strat: On a trend item, read the direction across ALL timepoints before judging the outcome.
questions.why: Albumin and prealbumin are the biochemical protein markers in the ABCD framework, and both values rise steadily across the three recorded timepoints. That consistent upward trend indicates improving protein status and shows the nutrition intervention is working. Both markers were clearly low on admission, ruling out the idea that no concern existed at the start.
whyNot: Both markers are rising, not falling, across the three timepoints, so protein status is improving rather than worsening.
Admission values of 2.6 g/dL albumin and 9 mg/dL prealbumin were clearly below normal, not within normal limits.
Albumin and prealbumin are protein markers, not renal markers, so they should be trended for nutrition status, not kidney function.

questions.stem: A client is receiving parenteral nutrition through a peripherally-inserted central catheter (PICC) line. Which complication should the nurse recognize as the most common and serious risk of this therapy?
opts: Catheter-related infection at the central line
Aspiration of the nutrition solution into the lungs
Clogging of the feeding tube lumen
Abdominal distention and cramping
questions.rat: The guide states infection of the catheter is the most common and serious complication of parenteral nutrition, which is why sterile technique is required for insertion and maintenance of the central line. Aspiration, tube clogging, and abdominal distention are complications of enteral (tube) feeding, which uses the GI tract — not of parenteral nutrition, which bypasses the GI system and is infused into the bloodstream.
questions.strat: Match the complication to the route: bloodstream access worries about infection; a gut tube worries about aspiration and GI upset.
questions.why: Infection of the catheter is the most common and serious complication of parenteral nutrition. This is why sterile technique is required for inserting and maintaining the central line. Parenteral nutrition infuses directly into the bloodstream, bypassing the GI system, so it does not carry the risks tied to tube feeding.
whyNot: Aspiration into the lungs is a complication of enteral tube feeding through the GI tract, not of parenteral nutrition.
A clogged feeding tube lumen is a mechanical problem specific to enteral tubes, which parenteral nutrition does not use.
Abdominal distention and cramping are GI complications of enteral feeding, since parenteral nutrition bypasses the GI tract entirely.

questions.stem:
CASE (1/6) Recognize cues. An 82-year-old client with dementia and difficulty swallowing is receiving a continuous nasogastric (NG) tube feeding. Two hours into the shift the nurse gathers the following data.

Which findings are relevant cues the nurse should note as the assessment proceeds? Select all that apply.
opts: The tube was placed because the client's upper GI tract is only partially functioning
The client has vomited a small amount of tube-feeding formula
A variety of enteral formulas are commercially available for tube feeding
The head of the bed has been lowered flat for linen changes and not raised again
The feedings are being counted as intake on the intake and output (I&O) record
The client is reporting nausea and the abdomen appears distended
questions.rat: Nausea, abdominal distention, and vomiting are GI complications of enteral feeding the guide lists, and a flat head of bed is a setup for aspiration during feeding — all are relevant cues. Counting feedings as I&O, the availability of many formulas, and the indication for tube placement are true background facts from the guide but are not abnormal cues that change the picture for this client.
questions.strat: A 'cue' is data that is abnormal or changes the plan — separate it from true-but-routine background information.
questions.why: Vomiting formula, a flat head of bed during feeding, and new nausea with abdominal distention are abnormal findings that change this client's plan of care. The flat bed is a direct setup for aspiration, while the vomiting and distention are GI complications the nurse must act on.
whyNot: The reason the tube was placed is true background information about this client, not a new abnormal cue.
That many enteral formulas exist commercially is a general fact about tube feeding, not a cue about this client.
Counting feedings as intake on the I&O record is routine documentation practice, not an abnormal finding to flag.

questions.stem: CASE (2/6) Analyze cues. The nurse links the cues together: the client has nausea, abdominal distention, vomited formula, and the head of the bed is flat. Which explanation best accounts for this cluster of findings?
opts: An expected response to continuous enteral feeding that needs no change
A catheter-related bloodstream infection from the central feeding access
Feeding intolerance with GI complications and aspiration risk
Dehydration caused by inadequate free-water intake through the tube
questions.rat: Nausea, distention, and vomiting are the GI complications of tube feeding the guide names, and with the head of the bed flat the vomited formula puts the client at risk for aspiration — together this is feeding intolerance. The access is an NG tube, not a central catheter, so bloodstream infection does not fit; vomiting formula is not an expected finding; and dehydration would not explain the nausea and distention.
questions.strat: Cluster the cues before naming the problem — GI upset plus a flat bed points to feeding intolerance.
questions.why: Nausea, abdominal distention, and vomited formula are the GI complications of tube feeding. With the head of the bed flat, that vomited formula also puts this client at risk for aspiration. Together, this cluster of findings best fits feeding intolerance with an added aspiration risk.
whyNot: Vomiting formula is not an expected response to continuous feeding, so this cluster does need a change in care.
The access here is a nasogastric tube, not a central catheter, so bloodstream infection does not fit these findings.
Dehydration from inadequate free water would not explain the nausea, distention, and vomiting seen in this cluster.

questions.stem: CASE (3/6) Prioritize hypotheses. Considering the client's vomiting of formula with the head of the bed flat, which concern should the nurse rank as the highest priority?
opts: Clogging of the nasogastric tube
Aspiration of formula into the airway
Slowed progress toward the client's weight goal
Diarrhea from the enteral formula
questions.rat: The guide repeatedly stresses positioning to prevent aspiration, and aspiration is the mechanical complication that threatens the airway — by an airway/safety framework it outranks the others. Diarrhea, a clogged tube, and slow weight gain are real enteral concerns from the guide but none is an immediate threat to airway or breathing.
questions.strat: When one hypothesis threatens the airway, it wins the priority — aspiration outranks GI tolerance and equipment issues.
questions.why: Aspiration is the mechanical complication that directly threatens this client's airway and breathing, and positioning is repeatedly emphasized as the way to prevent it. Under an airway-first safety framework, a threat to breathing always outranks GI tolerance or equipment problems that are not immediately life-threatening.
whyNot: A clogged tube is an equipment problem, not an immediate threat to this client's airway or breathing.
Slowed progress toward a weight goal is a real concern, but it is not an urgent threat to airway or breathing.
Diarrhea is a GI tolerance issue from the formula, not an immediate airway or breathing emergency.

questions.stem: CASE (4/6) Generate solutions (bowtie). Choose the central problem, two actions, and two parameters to monitor for this client — all drawn from safe enteral feeding practice.

opts: Deficient fluid volume from diuresis
Catheter-related bloodstream infection
Feeding intolerance with aspiration risk
Increase the feeding rate to meet the daily calorie goal sooner
Verify tube placement before giving any feeding or medication
Flush the tube with the parenteral solution to clear it
Place the client in a semi-Fowler's position during and after the feeding
Central line insertion site for redness
Head circumference
Gastric residual amount
Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal distention

questions.rat: The problem is feeding intolerance with aspiration risk. Safe enteral care from the guide means keeping the client in semi-Fowler's during and after feeding and verifying placement before instilling anything, while monitoring gastric residual (to prevent over-inflation of the stomach) and the GI tolerance signs of nausea, vomiting, and distention. A central-line site and head circumference belong to other situations, and raising the rate or flushing with parenteral solution are unsafe distractors.
questions.strat: In a bowtie, actions treat the named problem and parameters monitor it — keep every column tied together.
questions.why: The central problem is feeding intolerance with aspiration risk. Safe enteral practice means verifying tube placement before giving anything and keeping the client in semi-Fowler's position during and after the feeding. The nurse should then monitor gastric residual, which flags stomach over-inflation, along with nausea, vomiting, and distention, which flag GI intolerance.
whyNot: Deficient fluid volume from diuresis describes a different clinical picture, one driven by fluid loss rather than by feeding intolerance and aspiration risk.
Catheter-related bloodstream infection applies to central-line care for parenteral nutrition, not to this client's tube-feeding complications.

questions.stem: CASE (5/6) Take action. The nurse intervenes to manage the feeding intolerance and aspiration risk. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
opts: Lay the client flat to make them more comfortable during the feeding
Keep the head of the bed elevated in semi-Fowler's during and after the feeding
Continue the current rate without reassessing because feedings count as intake
Verify correct tube placement before resuming the feeding or giving medications
Check the gastric residual to prevent over-inflation of the stomach
questions.rat: Semi-Fowler's positioning during and after feeding, verifying placement before instilling anything, and checking gastric residual to prevent over-inflation are the safe-care steps the guide specifies for enteral feeding. Laying the client flat increases aspiration risk, and continuing unchanged ignores the intolerance — both are realistic but unsafe errors.
questions.strat: Tube-feeding safety: sit upright, confirm placement, and check residual before continuing.
questions.why: Keeping the head of the bed elevated in semi-Fowler's during and after the feeding protects the airway. Verifying tube placement before resuming feeding or giving medication confirms it is safe to proceed. Checking gastric residual before continuing confirms the stomach is not over-distended.
whyNot: Laying the client flat removes the upright positioning that protects the airway, raising rather than lowering aspiration risk.
Continuing the rate unchanged ignores signs of intolerance instead of reassessing before more formula is given.

questions.stem: CASE (6/6) Evaluate outcomes. After the nurse's interventions, which reassessment finding best indicates that the plan for this client is working?
opts: The gastric residual has increased compared with the value at the previous check
The client still reports mild nausea, although the abdomen is no longer distended
The client now tolerates the feeding with no nausea, vomiting, or distention
The feeding is now infusing at a noticeably faster rate than it was before
questions.rat: Resolution of the GI complications (no nausea, vomiting, or distention) with the client kept upright shows the feeding intolerance and aspiration risk are resolving — a monitoring-and-evaluation outcome from the guide. Persistent nausea is only a partial improvement, a faster rate does not show tolerance, and a rising residual signals worsening rather than improvement.
questions.strat: Judge the outcome against the original problem — look for the cues to have fully cleared, not just eased.
questions.why: The client now tolerates the feeding with no nausea, vomiting, or distention. This shows the feeding intolerance and aspiration risk have resolved while the client stays upright and monitored. Complete resolution, not partial improvement, is the outcome the plan was designed to achieve.
whyNot: A gastric residual that has increased signals worsening intolerance, not the improvement the plan was aiming for.
Persistent nausea even without distention shows only partial improvement, not full resolution of the feeding problem.
A faster infusion rate describes the mechanics of delivery and says nothing about whether the client is tolerating the feeding.

questions.stem: A client recovering from abdominal surgery is tolerating sips of water and is ready to begin oral intake. The nurse reviews the consistency progression. The first oral diet, used to maintain fluid balance with minimal digestive impact, allows [1]. As the client improves and is advanced to the next step, the diet may add [2].

blanks.label: [1] Clear liquid allowed item
opts: vanilla pudding
strained cream of mushroom soup
beef bouillon and gelatin

blanks.label: [2] First item added on full liquid
opts: smooth ice cream and custard
scrambled eggs
buttered white toast

questions.rat: A clear liquid diet allows liquids you can see through — broth, bouillon, gelatin, clear juice — to maintain fluid balance after surgery or vomiting. A full liquid diet is the next step and adds smooth dairy items such as ice cream, custards, and strained cream soups. Cream soup and pudding are full-liquid, not clear; eggs and toast are solids that belong to a soft or regular diet, several steps later.
questions.strat: If you can see through it, it's a clear liquid. Full liquid adds smooth dairy, still nothing you chew.
questions.why: A clear liquid diet allows only liquids you can see through, such as broth, bouillon, gelatin, and clear juice. This maintains fluid balance with minimal digestive work after surgery. The full liquid diet is the next progression step and adds smooth dairy items such as ice cream and custard, still requiring no chewing.

questions.stem: A client is being advanced from a clear liquid diet back toward a regular diet after an episode of acute gastroenteritis. Which sequence reflects the correct order of diet advancement?
opts: Clear liquid, then full liquid, then pureed/mechanical soft, then regular
Clear liquid, then regular, then full liquid, then pureed/mechanical soft
Clear liquid, then pureed/mechanical soft, then full liquid, then regular
Full liquid, then clear liquid, then regular, then pureed/mechanical soft
questions.rat: Diets are advanced from least to most digestive workload: clear liquid (see-through) to full liquid (smooth dairy added) to pureed/mechanical soft (food that needs little or no chewing) to regular. The other sequences place a thicker or harder-to-digest texture before an easier one, which is not how tolerance is built.
questions.strat: Advance thin-to-thick, easy-to-hard: clear, full, soft/pureed, regular.
questions.why: Diet advancement moves from least to most digestive workload. It goes from clear liquid, which is see-through, to full liquid, which adds smooth dairy. Next is pureed or mechanical soft food needing little or no chewing, then regular. Each step asks the healing gut to handle slightly more texture than the last.
whyNot: Placing regular food before full liquid and pureed textures skips straight to the heaviest digestive workload too soon.
Starting with full liquid then moving back to pureed or mechanical soft reverses the intended thin-to-thick progression.
Beginning with full liquid before clear liquid ignores the need to confirm fluid tolerance first.

questions.stem: A client who had a stroke was evaluated by speech therapy and placed on a mildly thick (IDDSI Level 2) liquid and minced-and-moist (Level 5) food diet for dysphagia. At lunch the nurse observes the client coughing and clearing the throat after each sip of the thickened juice and notices a wet, gurgly voice. Which action should the nurse take first?
opts: Encourage the client to drink faster to clear the liquid through quickly
Thin the juice with extra water so it slides down more easily for the client
Switch the client to thin liquids since the thick juice causes coughing
Stop the oral intake and keep the client upright to protect the airway
questions.rat: Coughing, throat-clearing, and a wet/gurgly voice are signs the thickened liquid is being aspirated; the priority is to stop intake and protect the airway (ABCs) before reassessing. Thinning the liquid or moving to thin liquids increases aspiration risk in dysphagia, and urging faster drinking worsens it.
questions.strat: Wet voice + coughing on liquids = aspiration. Stop feeding, protect the airway first; thin liquids are riskier, not safer.
questions.why: Coughing, throat-clearing, and a wet or gurgly voice after sipping thickened juice are signs the liquid is being aspirated. The nurse's priority is to stop oral intake and keep the client upright to protect the airway. This follows the airway-first approach used whenever aspiration is suspected, before reassessing further.
whyNot: Encouraging faster drinking gives the client less time to control the swallow and worsens the aspiration risk.
Thinning the juice with water removes the very thickening that was ordered to slow the liquid down.
Switching to thin liquids moves toward the consistency that is hardest for a dysphagia client to control safely.

questions.topic: Renal Diet — Foods Allowed vs. Avoid
questions.stem: A client on hemodialysis is learning to choose foods within a renal diet that limits potassium and phosphorus. For each food, classify it as one to encourage or one to limit/avoid on this diet.
questions.rat: Apples, berries, grapes, broccoli, carrots, and green beans are the lower-potassium choices the National Kidney Foundation lists to encourage. Bananas and orange juice are high-potassium fruit; dairy is high in phosphorus; potatoes and tomatoes are high-potassium vegetables; and salt substitutes are avoided because they contain potassium. All four are limited on a renal diet.
questions.strat: Renal diet limits potassium and phosphorus: dairy = phosphorus; banana, OJ, potato, tomato, salt substitute = potassium. Apples/berries/grapes and broccoli/carrots/green beans are the safe swaps.
questions.why: Apples, berries, grapes, broccoli, carrots, and green beans are the lower-potassium choices a renal diet encourages. Bananas and orange juice are high in potassium, and dairy is high in phosphorus. Potatoes and tomatoes are high-potassium vegetables, and salt substitutes are avoided because they contain potassium rather than sodium.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure and hypertension is being taught a low-sodium diet that pairs with the DASH approach. Which client statements indicate correct understanding? Select all that apply.
opts: "I'll switch from fresh chicken to canned ravioli and frozen dinners for convenience."
"I'll build meals around fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy."
"I'll season my food with herbs and spices instead of salt."
"Adding soy sauce instead of salt is a good low-sodium swap."
"I'll read the nutrition label, since most of my sodium comes from processed and prepared foods."
questions.rat: Using herbs/spices, reading labels (about 77% of sodium is from processed/prepared foods), and centering meals on fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy are all consistent with a low-sodium DASH pattern. Canned entrees and frozen dinners are named high-sodium foods, and soy sauce is explicitly high in sodium — both are common errors, not improvements.
questions.strat: Low sodium = fresh, label-read, herbs not salt. Canned/frozen/soy sauce are the hidden-salt traps.
questions.why: Building meals around fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy fits a low-sodium DASH pattern. So does seasoning with herbs and spices instead of salt, and reading nutrition labels. This matters because roughly three-quarters of the average person's daily sodium intake comes from processed and prepared foods.
whyNot: Switching to canned ravioli and frozen dinners trades fresh food for two of the highest-sodium convenience categories.
Soy sauce is itself a concentrated sodium source, so using it as a salt substitute defeats the purpose.

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with celiac disease asks the nurse which foods may contain hidden gluten. Which items should the nurse tell the client to check labels on or avoid? Select all that apply.
opts: Plain grilled chicken breast
Fresh apples and grapes
Canned soups and gravies
Soy sauce
Beer
questions.rat: Soy sauce, beer, and canned soups/gravies are listed as common sources of hidden gluten because they contain or are processed with wheat, barley, or malt. Plain chicken and fresh fruit are naturally gluten-free whole foods and do not require label-checking for gluten, so flagging them reflects over-restriction rather than the actual hidden-gluten risk.
questions.strat: Hidden gluten hides in processed liquids and sauces — soy sauce, beer, soups, gravy. Naturally single-ingredient whole foods are safe.
questions.why: Soy sauce, beer, and canned soups or gravies are common hidden sources of gluten, since they contain or are processed with wheat, barley, or malt. A client with celiac disease should check labels on these items or avoid them to prevent an inflammatory reaction in the small intestine.
whyNot: Plain grilled chicken breast is a naturally gluten-free whole food that does not need label-checking for gluten.
Fresh apples and grapes are naturally gluten-free produce, so flagging them reflects over-restriction rather than an actual hidden-gluten risk.

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes is using the Diabetes Plate Method and shows the nurse a photo of dinner: half the 9-inch plate is fried chicken, one quarter is white rice, and one quarter is buttered corn, with a regular soda. Which adjustment best aligns the meal with the plate method?
opts: Remove the protein entirely and replace that quarter with a second serving of rice
Fill half the plate with non-starchy vegetables and swap the soda for water
Double the rice and corn so the plate is mostly carbohydrate for energy
Keep the plate as is but add a large glass of fruit juice on the side
questions.rat: The Diabetes Plate Method fills half the plate with non-starchy vegetables, one quarter with lean protein, one quarter with carbohydrate, and pairs it with water or a low-calorie drink. This meal has no non-starchy vegetables and a sugary soda, so adding vegetables and switching to water is the correct fix. Removing protein, doubling carbohydrate, or adding juice all worsen the carbohydrate-to-vegetable balance and raise blood glucose.
questions.strat: Plate method: half non-starchy veggies, quarter lean protein, quarter carbs, water to drink.
questions.why: The Diabetes Plate Method fills half the plate with non-starchy vegetables, one quarter with lean protein, and one quarter with carbohydrate. It pairs this with water or a low-calorie drink. This dinner has no non-starchy vegetables and a sugary soda, so adding vegetables and swapping to water is the correct fix.
whyNot: Removing the protein entirely and adding more rice increases the carbohydrate share instead of restoring the vegetable half.
Doubling the rice and corn makes the plate mostly carbohydrate, which raises blood glucose rather than balancing it.
Adding fruit juice on the side stacks another sugary drink onto a meal that already lacks vegetables.

questions.stem: Two clients have new diet orders. Client A has an inflamed, irritated bowel after recent surgery; Client B is managing chronic constipation and hemorrhoids. Which plan correctly matches each diet to the client?
opts: Client A on a high-fiber diet with more fluids; Client B on a low-fiber (low-residue) diet
Both clients on a high-fiber diet to keep the bowel moving
Client A on a high-fiber diet with a fluid restriction; Client B on a low-residue diet
Client A on a low-fiber (low-residue) diet; Client B on a high-fiber diet with more fluids
questions.rat: A low-fiber/low-residue diet reduces stool bulk to rest an inflamed or post-surgical bowel, so it fits Client A; a high-fiber diet with at least eight glasses of fluid daily prevents constipation and hemorrhoids, so it fits Client B. Reversing them, or giving everyone high fiber, irritates the healing bowel; high fiber is also contraindicated with a fluid restriction.
questions.strat: Irritated bowel: rest with low residue. Constipation: high fiber plus fluids. Never pair high fiber with a fluid restriction.
questions.why: A low-fiber, low-residue diet reduces stool bulk to rest an inflamed or post-surgical bowel, which fits Client A. A high-fiber diet with at least eight glasses of fluid daily prevents constipation and hemorrhoids, which fits Client B. Matching the diet to the client depends on whether the bowel needs rest or stimulation.
whyNot: Putting Client A on high fiber with more fluids irritates a bowel that needs rest, and reverses the pairing.
Giving both clients a high-fiber diet ignores that Client A's healing bowel needs less bulk, not more.
Pairing high fiber with a fluid restriction for Client A is contraindicated, since high fiber requires extra fluids to work safely.

questions.stem: A client newly started on warfarin tells the nurse, "I eat a big spinach-and-kale salad most days, but I'll just cut all leafy greens out completely now." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
opts: "Leafy greens have no real effect on warfarin, so eat whatever amount you like."
"Try to keep your leafy-green intake about the same amount from day to day."
"Cutting greens out of your diet is the safest plan now that you take warfarin."
"Eat extra leafy greens so the added vitamin K makes the warfarin work harder."
questions.rat: Vitamin K is the antidote that opposes warfarin, so it is the day-to-day consistency of vitamin K intake — not avoidance — that keeps the INR stable; suddenly eliminating greens raises the warfarin effect just as suddenly bingeing lowers it. Cutting greens out or doubling them both swing the INR, and greens clearly do affect warfarin.
questions.strat: Warfarin + vitamin K = keep intake STEADY, not zero — big swings either way move the INR.
questions.why: Vitamin K opposes warfarin's effect, so keeping day-to-day intake of leafy greens about the same is what stabilizes the INR, not avoiding them altogether. Suddenly eliminating a food the client normally eats raises the warfarin effect just as suddenly bingeing on it would lower the effect.
whyNot: Saying leafy greens have no real effect on warfarin is inaccurate, since vitamin K directly opposes the drug.
Cutting greens out completely removes a source of vitamin K the client's dose has been stabilized around, which can swing the INR.
Eating extra greens to intensify the warfarin effect misunderstands the relationship, since more vitamin K opposes warfarin rather than strengthening it.

questions.stem: A client is being discharged on phenelzine, a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI), for depression. The nurse teaches the client to avoid tyramine-containing foods to prevent a hypertensive crisis. Which foods should the nurse instruct the client to avoid? Select all that apply.
opts: Fermented foods such as sauerkraut and soy sauce
Cured and smoked meats such as salami and pepperoni
Aged cheddar and blue cheese
Tap water and decaffeinated herbal tea
White rice and plain pasta
Fresh chicken breast cooked the same day
questions.rat: Tyramine accumulates in aged, cured, smoked, and fermented foods; with an MAOI blocking its breakdown, tyramine drives vasoconstriction and a hypertensive crisis. Freshly cooked meats, plain grains, and water are low in tyramine and are safe.
questions.strat: Tyramine = AGED / cured / fermented. "If it's been sitting and ripening, skip it on an MAOI."
questions.why: Tyramine accumulates in aged, cured, smoked, and fermented foods such as sauerkraut, soy sauce, salami, pepperoni, and aged or blue cheese. With an MAOI blocking tyramine's breakdown, eating these foods can trigger vasoconstriction and a hypertensive crisis, so the client should avoid all of them.
whyNot: Tap water and decaffeinated herbal tea contain essentially no tyramine and remain safe for this client to drink.
White rice and plain pasta are low-tyramine grains that do not require any restriction on an MAOI.
Fresh chicken breast cooked the same day has not had time to accumulate tyramine through aging or curing.

questions.stem: A client taking a statin reports drinking a large glass of grapefruit juice every morning with the medication. The nurse explains the interaction. Which statement best describes why this combination is a concern?
opts: Grapefruit blocks liver enzymes that break the drug down, so more drug stays active
Grapefruit speeds up the liver enzymes that break the drug down, so it is cleared too fast
Grapefruit binds the drug in the stomach and carries it out before much is absorbed
Grapefruit changes the drug's chemical structure so it gradually loses its effect
questions.rat: Grapefruit inhibits the cytochrome P450 enzymes that metabolize many drugs, so the drug is broken down more slowly, accumulates, and can reach toxic levels — with statins this raises the risk of muscle injury. It does not induce (speed up) metabolism, chelate the drug, or chemically inactivate it.
questions.strat: Grapefruit jams CYP450 → drug piles up → toxicity. Think "blocked enzyme = higher drug level."
questions.why: Grapefruit inhibits the cytochrome P450 enzymes that metabolize many drugs. As a result, the statin is broken down more slowly, accumulates in the blood, and can reach toxic levels. With statins, this buildup raises the risk of muscle injury rather than simply changing how the drug is absorbed or shaped.
whyNot: Grapefruit does not speed up these liver enzymes, so it does not clear the drug faster than normal.
Grapefruit does not bind the drug in the stomach and carry it out before absorption occurs.
Grapefruit does not alter the drug's chemical structure or cause it to gradually lose its effect.

questions.stem: A client is prescribed an oral tetracycline antibiotic and asks the nurse how to take it. The client routinely drinks a glass of milk and takes a calcium supplement at breakfast. Which instruction should the nurse give?
opts: Take the antibiotic together with the milk and calcium to protect the stomach lining
Stop the calcium supplement and avoid all dairy for the entire course of antibiotics
Separate the antibiotic from milk and the calcium supplement by a couple of hours
Take the calcium supplement at the exact same time so both are absorbed together
questions.rat: Tetracyclines (and fluoroquinolones) bind calcium in a chelation reaction that blocks the antibiotic's absorption, so the client should space the antibiotic and any calcium/dairy by a couple of hours rather than taking them together. Taking them together reduces absorption; stopping calcium entirely is unnecessary when timing alone solves the problem.
questions.strat: Calcium grabs the -cycline/-floxacin → separate the doses; you space them, you don't stop the calcium.
questions.why: Tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones bind calcium through a chelation reaction that blocks the antibiotic from being absorbed. Because of this, the client should separate the antibiotic from milk or a calcium supplement by a couple of hours. Timing alone solves the problem without requiring the client to give up calcium altogether.
whyNot: Taking the antibiotic together with milk and calcium lets the chelation reaction block absorption right away.
Stopping the calcium supplement and all dairy for the whole course is more restrictive than necessary when timing alone fixes the interaction.
Taking the calcium at the exact same time guarantees the two will bind together instead of absorbing separately.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a client newly prescribed levothyroxine how to take it. The client also takes a calcium and iron supplement. Which instruction reflects correct administration?
opts: Take it whenever it is convenient, since meal timing has no effect on how it is absorbed
Take it at bedtime right after the calcium and iron, with a light snack to settle it
Take it with breakfast alongside the calcium and iron so the food prevents stomach upset
Take it on an empty stomach before breakfast, apart from the calcium and iron
questions.rat: Levothyroxine absorption is unpredictable with food, so it is taken on an empty stomach 30–60 minutes before eating; calcium and iron bind it and must be separated by several hours. Taking it with food or alongside calcium/iron reduces absorption, and the timing very much matters.
questions.strat: Levothyroxine = empty stomach, before breakfast, away from calcium/iron.
questions.why: Levothyroxine's absorption is unpredictable when taken with food, so it should be taken on an empty stomach 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast. Calcium and iron bind the hormone and must be separated from it by several hours. Taking them together or alongside food reduces how much of the dose is absorbed.
whyNot: Taking it whenever is convenient ignores that meal timing changes how much of the dose is absorbed.
Taking it at bedtime right after calcium and iron pairs it with the very supplements that bind it.
Taking it with breakfast alongside calcium and iron lets food and the supplements both blunt absorption.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews food and medication interactions with a client who takes several drugs. Match each medication to the correct teaching point the nurse should give.
shared: Take with food or milk to reduce stomach irritation
Take on an empty stomach, well before food, for reliable absorption
Keep day-to-day vitamin K (leafy green) intake consistent
Avoid grapefruit juice, which can raise the drug to toxic levels
questions.rat: Aspirin and NSAIDs irritate the gastric lining, so food or milk buffers them; levothyroxine needs an empty stomach for predictable absorption; warfarin's effect is opposed by vitamin K, so leafy-green intake should stay steady; grapefruit inhibits the enzymes that clear many statins, raising drug levels.
questions.strat: Sort by the mechanism: irritant→food, absorption-sensitive→empty stomach, antidote-food→keep steady, enzyme-blocker→avoid.
questions.why: Aspirin and NSAIDs irritate the gastric lining, so taking them with food or milk buffers that effect. Levothyroxine needs an empty stomach for predictable absorption. Warfarin's effect is opposed by vitamin K, so leafy-green intake should stay consistent day to day. Grapefruit inhibits the enzymes that clear many statins, raising drug levels toward toxicity.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old client has taken digoxin with water for several months with good results. At a clinic visit a low calcium level is found, and a calcium supplement is added without a full medication review. Two weeks later the client returns to the emergency department with nausea, visual changes, and a slow, irregular pulse. Which conclusion best explains this client's presentation?
opts: The findings are unrelated to medications and reflect normal aging of the heart
The calcium supplement blocked digoxin absorption, so the client is showing signs of an under-dose
Adding calcium without reviewing the interaction with digoxin contributed to digoxin toxicity
The calcium corrected the deficiency, and these are the expected effects of a normal calcium level
questions.rat: The client shows classic digoxin toxicity (nausea, visual changes, bradydysrhythmia); calcium was added without a medication review that would have flagged its interaction with digoxin, so the missed interaction contributed to toxicity. The presentation is excess effect, not an under-dose, is clearly medication-related rather than normal aging, and these are not expected effects of a normal calcium level.
questions.strat: New drug + old drug + a sick patient = suspect the interaction. A skipped med review sets up toxicity.
questions.why: The nausea, visual changes, and slow, irregular pulse are classic signs of digoxin toxicity. The calcium supplement was added without a full medication review. Because that review was skipped, the interaction between calcium and digoxin was missed, contributing to toxicity rather than an under-dose.
whyNot: The findings are not normal aging, since this specific symptom pattern points to a medication effect, not an age-related change.
Calcium does not block digoxin absorption here, so the presentation reflects excess drug effect rather than an under-dose.
These symptoms are not the expected effects of a normal calcium level, since they signal toxicity from the interaction instead.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a 30-year-old client who is 24 weeks pregnant about foods to avoid because of her higher risk for serious foodborne illness. The client lists several lunch options she enjoys. Which choice should the nurse advise her to avoid?
opts: A firm hard-boiled egg she peels and eats with whole-grain crackers
A turkey sandwich layered with unpasteurized soft cheese
A fresh apple she rinses well under cool running water before eating
A cup of pasteurized plain yogurt topped with rinsed fresh berries
questions.rat: Pregnant clients are a high-risk group; unpasteurized (raw-milk) soft cheese can carry Listeria, which crosses the placenta and threatens the fetus, so it should be avoided. Washed produce, pasteurized yogurt, and a fully cooked egg are safe and encouraged — they are distractors because clients may overgeneralize 'avoid dairy, fruit, and eggs.'
questions.strat: In pregnancy, the unpasteurized or raw item is the one to cut, not the cooked or pasteurized food.
questions.why: Pregnant clients are a high-risk group for serious foodborne illness, and unpasteurized soft cheese can carry Listeria, which crosses the placenta and threatens the fetus. This sandwich should be avoided, while a well-washed apple, pasteurized yogurt, and a fully cooked egg remain safe, recommended choices during pregnancy.
whyNot: A firm hard-boiled egg is fully cooked and peeled, so it carries no meaningful Listeria risk.
A fresh apple rinsed well under running water is a washed whole food that is safe to eat.
Pasteurized yogurt topped with rinsed fresh berries pairs two low-risk, properly handled foods and remains safe.

questions.stem: A nurse reviewing food safety identifies a food most commonly linked to each foodborne organism. Match each organism to the food it is most often associated with in an outbreak.
questions.rat: Salmonella is classically tied to eggs, Campylobacter to raw poultry, norovirus and Vibrio to raw shellfish, and Listeria to unpasteurized milk and soft cheeses. The foods are similar 'raw/animal-source' choices, so the match rests on knowing each organism's signature high-risk food rather than guessing.
questions.strat: Anchor each bug to its signature food: Salmonella-eggs, Campylobacter-poultry, norovirus-shellfish, Listeria-raw dairy.
questions.why: Salmonella is classically linked to eggs, and Campylobacter to raw poultry. Norovirus and Vibrio are linked to raw oysters and shellfish, and Listeria to unpasteurized milk and soft cheeses. Because the food choices are similar raw, animal-source options, matching each organism correctly depends on knowing its signature high-risk food rather than guessing by category.

questions.stem: At a family picnic, a nurse notices a tray of cooked chicken has been sitting on a buffet table in the sun for about 3 hours at roughly 85 °F (29 °C). The host asks whether the chicken is still safe to eat. Which response by the nurse is best?
opts: "Throw it out — food left over 2 hours in the danger zone grows bacteria."
"It is perfectly safe to eat, since it was thoroughly cooked all the way through earlier this same afternoon."
"It is fine to keep serving as long as no one has noticed an off smell or any change in its color yet."
"Just reheat it in the microwave for a minute or two and it will be perfectly safe to serve again."
questions.rat: Bacteria multiply rapidly between 40 °F and 140 °F (the danger zone); perishable food held there longer than 2 hours should be discarded. Thorough earlier cooking does not protect food that later sits warm, reheating does not undo toxin buildup, and many pathogens produce no change in smell, color, or taste — these are common reasoning errors.
questions.strat: Time + temperature, not appearance: over 2 hours in the 40-140 °F danger zone means discard it.
questions.why: Bacteria multiply rapidly between 40°F and 140°F, the temperature danger zone. Perishable food held there longer than two hours should be discarded regardless of how it looks or smells. Three hours in the sun at roughly 85°F falls well past that safe window for the chicken.
whyNot: Being thoroughly cooked earlier in the day does not protect food that later sits warm for hours.
The absence of an off smell or color change is not reassuring, since many pathogens cause neither.
Reheating in the microwave does not undo bacterial toxins that may have already built up while sitting out.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client the four steps to prevent foodborne illness — clean, separate, cook, and chill. Which client statements indicate correct understanding? Select all that apply.
opts: "I will keep my refrigerator at or below 40 °F (4 °C)."
"I will rinse the raw chicken under the faucet before I cook it."
"I will reuse the marinade from the raw beef as a sauce without boiling it."
"I will store raw chicken on the bottom shelf, below ready-to-eat foods."
"I will use separate cutting boards for raw meat and for fresh produce."
"I will refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours of cooking."
questions.rat: Refrigerating within 2 hours, using separate boards, storing raw meat below ready-to-eat food, and keeping the fridge at or below 40 °F all follow clean-separate-cook-chill. Rinsing raw poultry actually splashes bacteria around the sink and is not recommended, and reusing raw-meat marinade without boiling it transfers live pathogens onto cooked food — both are frequent, plausible mistakes.
questions.strat: Food-safety wrong answers usually spread contamination rather than prevent it — check whether each action adds or removes risk.
questions.why: Keeping the refrigerator at or below 40°F and storing raw chicken on the bottom shelf below ready-to-eat food both prevent cross-contamination. Using separate cutting boards for meat and produce, and refrigerating leftovers within two hours, complete the clean-separate-cook-chill framework for preventing foodborne illness.
whyNot: Rinsing raw chicken under the faucet splashes bacteria around the sink instead of removing it safely.
Reusing raw beef marinade as a sauce without boiling it first transfers live pathogens onto cooked food.
